documents: Le, Yang & Morgan (2022), Seismic constraints on crustal and uppermost mantle structure beneath the Hawaiian Swell, JGR Solid Earth 127, e2021JB023822 (published PDF, 25 pp.)

entry.evidence: Nevertheless, characteristics of interactions between the rising plume and its overlying migrating oceanic plate remain poorly understood; many outstanding questions still exist.

steps.action: Pose the open question of how the Hawaiian plume interacts with the overriding plate, including the origin of the swell and the role of the fracture zone in North Arch volcanism.
steps.quote: characteristics of interactions between the rising plume and its overlying migrating oceanic plate remain poorly understood

steps.action: List the published rival mechanisms for the swell and for North Arch volcanism: dynamic support, thermal rejuvenation, refracted plume, restite root, metasomatic underplating, flexural decompression, and restite-root migration across the MFZ.
steps.quote: Proposed mechanisms to create a hotspot swell include dynamic support

steps.action: Ask how much magmatic underplating thickens the crust, noting that contour-based active-source and receiver-function estimates assume a pure-melt layer and are spatially limited.
steps.quote: Therefore, to date, the amount of magmatic thickening of the crust beneath the island chain remains poorly constrained.

steps.action: Design a joint ambient-noise and teleseismic Rayleigh-wave approach at shorter periods (8–50 s) than earlier PLUME studies, so as to resolve the 10–70 km lithosphere.
steps.quote: By going to shorter periods (8–50 s) of Rayleigh waves than in previous studies that used the same dataset

steps.action: Process the existing PLUME records (54 usable OBSs plus land stations): ambient-noise cross-correlations after Bensen et al. with SNR and wavelength cuts, and teleseismic amplitude and phase with SNR thresholds and beamforming coherence selection (threshold 0.60).
steps.quote: Ultimately, we obtained ∼900 phase velocity dispersion curves for each period in the range of 8–25 s

steps.action: Invert for phase-velocity maps (two-step reweighted ANT; TPWT with 2-D kernels; 80 km correlation length chosen in trials), merge the two dispersion sets with normalized weights, and invert each node for 1-D Vs from a 2-D CRUST1.0/IASP91 starting model.
steps.quote: we combine the short period (8–25 s) phase velocities from ambient noise tomography (ANT) and longer period (18–50s) phase velocities from TPWT

steps.action: Test how the mismatch between actual and CRUST1.0 water depths affects the Vs inversion (Figure S3).
steps.quote: found that the crustal model starts to show significant changes only in for nodes where the water depth difference reaches

steps.action: Rerun the Vs inversion with a Bayesian Monte Carlo method and a different initial model (mantle similar, crust differs); run checkerboard tests at 250 and 150 km for ANT and TPWT with added noise; map posterior errors and set interpretation thresholds.
steps.quote: we performed standard checkerboard resolution tests for both ANT and TPWT

steps.action: Report phase-velocity results: fast anomalies tied to island topography at 8–10 s, a large low-velocity body beneath the islands at 18–50 s, and a smaller slow anomaly north of the MFZ.
steps.quote: a large low-velocity body located beneath the center of islands at periods of 18–50 s

steps.action: Compare the ANT and TPWT maps at the overlapping periods (18–25 s) and find similar patterns.
steps.quote: The consistency of the results obtained from two different methods with different datasets suggests that our study can reliably

steps.action: State that alternative Vs values or approaches for defining the crust do not change the crustal thickness variations significantly.
steps.quote: We note other values or using different approaches to define the crust will not change the resulting crustal thickness variations significantly.

steps.action: Describe the 3-D Vs model: thick crust beneath the chain and the NAVF, a shallow slow body beneath the North Arch, an elongated slow anomaly at 50–90 km, a slow vertical channel at the MFZ, a fast lid at 30–50 km, and a fast ring below 50 km.
steps.quote: The location of this low-velocity channel coincides with the spatial location of the MFZ

steps.action: Compare the crust and mantle model with receiver-function, compliance, active-source and earlier PLUME surface-wave and body-wave models, noting agreements and differences such as thicker crust near the NAVF and a non-uniform uppermost mantle.
steps.quote: It is thus worthwhile to compare our model with their results in order to highlight the similarities and distinctive features.

steps.action: Introduce a fractional-underplating estimator that interpolates Vs between assumed lower-crust (3.9 km/s) and uppermost-mantle (4.4 km/s) values, replacing the pure-melt contour assumption.
steps.quote: we use the velocity anomaly associated with the thickened lower crust relative to the average uppermost mantle velocity

steps.action: Map the equivalent underplating thickness (5–7 km along the chain, 4 km beneath the NAVF), compute an underplated volume of 1.81–2.19 × 10^6 km3 for original crust of 7–6.5 km, and derive the average magma flux over 5.1 Myr.
steps.quote: the average flux of magma for the Hawaiian hotspot is estimated to be within the range of 0.51–0.58

steps.action: Show the underplating depth and thickness from the constant 4.2 km/s cut-off alongside the fractional method (Figure 11).
steps.quote: The underplating determined by different methods.

steps.action: Compare the derived flux (16.1–18.5 m3/s) with published volcanic flux estimates (8–22 m3/s), concluding it is about twice previous minimum estimates.
steps.quote: previous studies inferred that the volcanic flux had been 8–22 m3

steps.action: Draw on Yamamoto and Morgan's (2009) 3-D numerical experiments (Morgan is a co-author here), in which restite-root spreading toward younger lithosphere across the MFZ reproduces NAVF volcanism.
steps.quote: Scenarios in which plume-melt-extraction led to the creation of a buoyant and more viscous restite-root

steps.action: Compare the thickened crust and low velocities beneath the North Arch with the location of off-chain volcanism predicted by the restite-root model.
steps.quote: consistent with the location of the off-chain volcanism predicted by the restite-root scenario of Yamamoto and Morgan (2009)

steps.action: Keep the restite-root explanation as favored, while noting that small-scale convection is not precluded.
steps.quote: [...] the hypothesis that plume melt-extraction created a restite-root that supports the anomalous relief of the Hawaiian swell.

steps.action: Reject the propagating-fracture model, which predicts a deep source beneath each island, because the anomaly is elongated with only one end reaching the deep mantle.
steps.quote: This observation contradicts an alternative magma-generation model by a propagating fracture (Natland & Winterer, 2005)

steps.action: Derive the lithospheric thickness and LAB velocity gradient expected under thermal rejuvenation, the refracted plume, and the restite root.
steps.quote: In the thermal rejuvenation hypothesis, the lower lithosphere should have been completely removed beneath the swell region

steps.action: Compare 1-D Vs profiles at four sites with these expectations: LAB at about 55 km and a trend of smoothing gradients, while noting the limited gradient resolution of surface waves.
steps.quote: the LABs of four locations are at about 55 km deep on average, shallower than the normal oceanic setting at 100 Ma age.

steps.action: Judge the refracted-plume hypothesis contradicted by the thin lithosphere, and thermal rejuvenation as predicting more thinning than observed.
steps.quote: which the refracted plume hypothesis appears to also contradict with

steps.action: Slightly favor the restite-root interpretation for the swell.
steps.quote: we slightly favor this interpretation

steps.action: Compare the LAB depths with Laske et al., Rychert et al. and Li et al., and compare Hawaii's crustal and underplating signals with other oceanic hotspots and volcanic margins.
steps.quote: The even deeper LAB (110 km) estimate of Li et al. (2004) may have been affected by their relatively poor data coverage.

steps.action: Conclude with a magma production rate of 0.5–0.6 km3/yr over 5 Ma and the lithospheric-modification findings.
steps.quote: We determine that magma production rates varied between 0.5 and 0.6 km3

end.claim: The shallow lithospheric structure (an elongated sub-lithospheric slow anomaly, a slow body beneath the North Arch offset across the MFZ, and thin lithosphere) is best explained by a restite swell root that erodes the lithospheric base and spreads preferentially beneath the younger side of the MFZ.

decisive_move.sentence: The joint inversion of short-period ambient-noise and teleseismic phase velocities into a 3-D Vs model of the 10–70 km lithosphere supplies every observation the interpretations and flux estimate rest on.

gates.evidence: Action: the data were reused from the PLUME experiment, collected for other aims; the authors' choice of period band was driven by imaging depth, not by a rival hypothesis. Claim: the observed lithospheric thinning could have contradicted the restite root and does contradict the refracted plume and propagating-fracture models (pp. 18-19), but the authors admit the LAB gradient is poorly resolved and that small-scale convection is not precluded. Registration: nothing is reported as fixed before the data were analysed.

imports.item: Ambient noise cross-correlation theory (Roux et al. 2005, J. Acoust. Soc. Am.) for the asymmetry of noise correlation functions
Simulated annealing (Press et al., Numerical Recipes) for estimating two-plane-wave parameters
Bayesian Monte Carlo inversion as an alternative Vs inversion

novelty_claims.quote: The magma emplacement volume associated with Hawaii is also more accurately estimated than in previous studies.
A thinned crust between the island chain and the NAVF is not seen in previous models.
This feature is more clearly imaged in our model
an inferred magma production rate that is twice that of previous minimum estimates.
average rates that are significantly higher than most previous estimates.

limits: Only the published PDF was supplied; the supplement (Figures S1-S7, the Monte Carlo inversion and the Vs uncertainties) and the review history were not, although the acknowledgments mention an associate editor and two anonymous reviewers. No review sequence is coded. The data were collected by the PLUME experiment, not by the authors. The restite-root numerical predictions (Yamamoto & Morgan 2009) come from a co-author's earlier work and are coded as inherited. The authors state that the LAB gradient, which is key to separating thermal rejuvenation from the restite root, is poorly resolved by surface waves, and that the LAB depth is an imprecise estimate. Sub-claims and their statuses: the magma flux of 0.51–0.58 km3/yr is estimate_with_resolution, but its range reflects only the assumed original crustal thickness (6.5–7 km), not the Vs uncertainty or the assumed end-member velocities (3.9 and 4.4 km/s), so its uncertainty is under-characterized (inference). The low-velocity channel at the MFZ and MFZ redistribution of melt are best_explanation. The 3-D Vs model is capability_characterized, at about 150–250 km lateral resolution. The crustal model differs between initial models, so the crust-based underplating volumes depend on the choice of a 2-D initial model, a choice the authors justify by geological plausibility rather than a test (inference).

disagreements.target: Leahy et al. (2010) receiver-function crustal thickness
disagreements.support: The Vs model gives a crust several km thicker beneath and north of the chain, and the authors attribute the difference to the station-only coverage of receiver functions.
disagreements.quote: the inferred crustal thickness is several kilometers thicker beneath the island chain and north of the island chain, in particular [...]

disagreements.target: Leahy et al. (2010) correlation of underplating with swell bathymetry
disagreements.support: Argued from the sparse station distribution, not from new data.
disagreements.quote: the sparse distribution of their stations, especially at the periphery of the swell, may bias this finding

disagreements.target: Doran and Laske (2021) compliance and ambient-noise model
disagreements.support: Their method resolves structure only beneath stations, so it cannot show lateral variations.
disagreements.quote: the structure in their model is confined to beneath the station locations due to a limitation of their method

disagreements.target: Velocity-contour definition of underplating in active-source and receiver-function studies
disagreements.support: Argues that intruded sills mix with peridotite, and replaces the contour with a fractional-velocity estimator.
disagreements.quote: This approach is based on the assumption that all materials in the layer are formed by melts, which is often unlikely to be true.

disagreements.target: Laske et al. (2011) uppermost mantle model
disagreements.support: The shorter ambient-noise periods resolve a high-velocity layer near 40 km and slow anomalies shifted along the MFZ.
disagreements.quote: Instead of a uniform structure at the uppermost mantle, our model shows strong velocity variations in that depth range

disagreements.target: Previous Hawaiian volcanic flux estimates (8–22 m3/s)
disagreements.support: Including the underplated volume (about twice the erupted volume) raises the flux to 16.1–18.5 m3/s.
disagreements.quote: an inferred magma production rate that is twice that of previous minimum estimates

disagreements.target: Flexural arch decompression for North Arch volcanism (Moore 1987; Bianco et al. 2005)
disagreements.support: A magnitude argument that flexural decompression is small, plus the observed slow body linked to the MFZ.
disagreements.quote: the few hundred meters of ‘decompression’ potentially associated with arch flexure is quite modest

disagreements.support: The elongated slow anomaly has only one end reaching the deep mantle, not a source beneath each island.
disagreements.quote: This observation contradicts an alternative magma-generation model by a propagating fracture (Natland & Winterer, 2005)

disagreements.support: The LAB at about 55 km and the absolute Vs indicate thinner lithosphere than the refracted plume predicts.
disagreements.quote: which the refracted plume hypothesis appears to also contradict with

disagreements.support: The observed thinning is less extreme than predicted, and the smoothing gradient trend fits erosion better.
disagreements.quote: The ‘thermal rejuvenation’ hypothesis would predict enhanced lithospheric thinning more extreme than that observed

disagreements.target: Li et al. (2004) LAB depth of about 110 km
disagreements.support: The surface-wave LAB is much shallower, and the authors attribute Li et al.'s value to poor data coverage.
disagreements.quote: The even deeper LAB (110 km) estimate of Li et al. (2004) may have been affected by their relatively poor data coverage.

disagreements.target: Rychert et al. (2013) 75 km boundary and LAB interpretation
disagreements.support: The boundary is absent beneath the chain, and the authors reinterpret it as the base of a thin restite root or a melt-ponding boundary.
disagreements.quote: The 75 km depth boundary found by Rychert et al. (2013) is absent directly beneath the island chain
